theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Your team must run conduit through 12 concrete-block walls in a school in Old Harbour. What should be done before any power tool is used?
options: Buy the cheapest drill bits so that the job costs less
Do a risk assessment and plan the tools, access and dust control
Start drilling early so the noise is over before lunch
Let each worker bring along and use whatever tools they own at home

questions.stem: Which tool is best for drilling 32 mm holes for conduit through a 150 mm concrete-block wall?
options: A cordless drill-driver fitted with a wood spade bit
An angle grinder fitted with a cutting disc
An impact driver with a steel twist drill
A rotary hammer with an SDS masonry bit or core bit

questions.stem: A 110 mm hole must be cut through a reinforced concrete wall for a cable duct. Which tool suits this best?
options: A diamond core drill, used as the maker says
A large bi-metal hole saw in a cordless drill
A hammer drill with a 13 mm masonry bit
An angle grinder used to cut a square opening

questions.stem: Which tool cuts a straight, square end on lengths of steel strut channel quickly and with few sparks?
options: An angle grinder with a grinding disc
A hacksaw with a coarse wood blade
A portable band saw with a metal blade
A jigsaw fitted with a fine wood-cutting blade

questions.stem: Why should a wall chaser be used with an extraction vacuum attached?
options: To keep the chaser's blades from going blunt
To make the chase deeper than the blades can cut
To capture fine silica dust that harms the lungs
To cool the motor so it can run all day long

questions.stem: When drilling and chasing concrete indoors, which mask gives suitable protection, along with dust extraction?
options: A close-fitting dust respirator of the right rating
A loose cotton cloth tied over the nose and mouth
A thin paper mask taken from the first-aid box
No mask, as long as a window is open

questions.stem: A rotary hammer's bit jams on a steel bar inside a wall. What does the tool's slip clutch help to prevent?
options: The bit breaking through the far side of the wall
The battery running down before the hole is done
The hammer action stopping on soft materials
The tool body twisting hard and hurting your wrist

questions.stem: When should the hammer action be switched off on a rotary hammer?
options: When drilling into hard concrete or stone
When drilling into tiles, timber or steel
When the bit is larger than 10 mm across
When the drill is used on a ceiling

questions.stem: Before core drilling through a floor slab, why should the slab be scanned and the drawings checked?
options: Cutting a live cable, pipe or steel tendon could be deadly
Scanning first makes the diamond core bit cut much faster
The drill will not start until the slab is scanned
It is only needed if the client asks for it

questions.stem: A wet diamond core drill is to be used. Which electrical precaution matters most?
options: Use an extension lead taped at every joint
Stand in the water so the drill stays earthed
Use RCD or GFCI protection, as the maker says
Keep the water running over the motor to cool it

questions.stem: A 1 500 W, 110 V tool is run from an extension lead rated 10 A. What is the problem?
options: None, because watts and amps are not related
The tool draws about 14 A, more than the lead's rating
The lead will make the tool run 10% faster
The tool will draw only 10 A and then stop working

questions.stem: Before use, a team member finds that the plug on a drill has been swapped for a cracked one held together with tape. What should happen?
options: Use it carefully, since it still works
Wrap more tape around it to make it stronger
Use it only for small jobs from now on
Tag it out of use and send it for repair

questions.stem: Why are portable power tools given a formal inspection and electrical test at set intervals, as well as the user's own check?
options: So that the tools can be sold for a higher price
So the user no longer needs to check them daily
So the maker's guarantee is extended each time
Some faults, such as a broken earth, cannot be seen

questions.stem: How should spare lithium-ion tool batteries be carried in a tool bag?
options: Loose among screws and drill bits so they stay cool
With terminal covers on, away from loose metal items
Wrapped in a damp cloth to stop them overheating
Fully charged and taped together in a bundle

questions.stem: Why should an impact driver not be used to tighten small terminal screws in a socket outlet or breaker?
options: It turns far too slowly for such small screws
It only works with left-hand threads
Its high torque can strip or crack the terminal
It cannot hold a normal screwdriver bit in its chuck

questions.stem: A breaker's maker gives a tightening torque for its terminals. Which tool should be used?
options: A torque screwdriver set to the maker's figure
An impact driver set on its highest speed setting
Any screwdriver, turned as hard as possible
Long-nose pliers gripping the screw head

questions.stem: A battery hydraulic crimping tool is used on large cable lugs. What must be checked before crimping?
options: That the lug is one size bigger than the cable
That the die matches the lug and cable size
That the battery is nearly flat to limit force
That the insulation is left on under the lug

questions.stem: Why must you keep your fingers out of the jaws of a hydraulic cutter or crimper when it is triggered?
options: It closes with huge force and will not stop for a hand
The jaws get hot enough to burn the skin on your fingers
The jaws spin round when the tool runs
It gives an electric shock through the jaws

questions.stem: An existing cable must be cut with a cable cutter during alterations. What must be done first?
options: Check the cutter's blades are sharp, then cut
Cut it quickly so that any arc is very short
Prove the cable dead and identify it at both ends
Wear rubber gloves, then cut it while it is in use

questions.stem: When a threading machine cuts threads on steel conduit, why is cutting oil applied?
options: To make the conduit lighter to carry on site
To stop the conduit from rusting for years
To let the machine run without a foot switch
To cool the dies and give a clean, sharp thread

questions.stem: Why do threading machines have a foot switch that stops the machine as soon as it is released?
options: So the operator can stop it at once if caught
So both hands are free to hold the oil can
So the machine uses less power while idle
So it can be left running while unattended

questions.stem: While cutting a 40 mm hole in a metal enclosure with a hole saw, the saw keeps snagging and jerking. What is the most likely cause?
options: The enclosure is made of very soft steel
The pilot drill is longer than the hole saw
The drill is on a low speed with a steady feed
Speed too high, or the work not held firmly

questions.stem: When cutting with a reciprocating saw, why should its shoe be held firmly against the work?
options: To make the blade run hotter and so cut faster
To stop the saw jumping and the blade snapping
To keep the battery from losing its charge too soon
To stop sawdust from falling on the floor

questions.stem: Which is the safest way to cut a steel strap fixing on site with an angle grinder?
options: Hold the strap in one hand and the grinder in the other
Remove the guard so you can see the line more clearly
Clamp the work, fit the guard and use a cutting disc
Use a grinding disc on its edge for a thinner cut

questions.stem: An angle grinder must be used in a ceiling space above timber and insulation. What should be arranged first?
options: Nothing, as sparks go out quickly in a ceiling
Spray water into the ceiling space while cutting
A hot-work permit, fire watch and an extinguisher
A larger disc so that the job is done faster

questions.stem: Who may use a powder-actuated (cartridge) fixing tool on site?
options: Anyone who has watched it being used once
Only a person trained and authorised to use it
Any electrician, as long as gloves are worn
Only the youngest member of the team

questions.stem: Why must a cartridge fixing tool never be fired into very hard or brittle material, such as glazed tile?
options: The fixing can ricochet or the material can shatter
The tool will not fire unless the surface is soft
The cartridge will be wasted without fixing anything
The tile will be marked and cost more to replace

questions.stem: A rotary hammer and a wall chaser are used all day in a small room. Which is the best control for the noise?
options: Turn up a radio so the noise is less noticeable
Work faster to finish before anyone complains
Use only one ear plug so you can still hear people
Wear hearing protection and limit the time exposed

questions.stem: Which sign may show that a worker is being harmed by vibration from power tools?
options: Sunburn on the backs of the hands
A sore throat at the end of the day
Red eyes after a long shift
Tingling, numbness or white fingers

questions.stem: You are drilling a ceiling from a mobile platform. Why should the drill be secured with a tool lanyard?
options: So it cannot fall and hit someone below
So it is easier to plug into the outlet
So it can be carried without a tool bag
So the drill runs at a steadier speed

questions.stem: When drilling up into a concrete ceiling with a rotary hammer, which helps most?
options: Pushing as hard as you can with arms fully stretched
Using the drill without its depth stop or side handle
Working from a stable platform at a comfortable height
Standing on the top step of a stepladder to get more reach

questions.stem: Why is the depth stop set before drilling holes for wall plugs?
options: To make the drill spin faster in soft walls
So the hole is deep enough but not too deep
To stop the bit from wearing out so quickly
So that the hammer action switches on

questions.stem: Why should an SDS bit's shank be lightly greased before it goes into the chuck?
options: To stop the bit falling out of the chuck
To reduce wear on the bit and the chuck
To help the bit cut through steel bars
To keep the dust from sticking to the wall

questions.stem: Which task should be left to a competent repairer, not done by the user?
options: Wiping dust off the casing with a dry cloth
Fitting a new drill bit with the tool unplugged
Replacing a damaged cable or opening the motor
Checking the cable and plug for damage

questions.stem: Which tool is best for making a clean 20 mm hole in the side of a steel enclosure that is already fixed to a wall?
options: An angle grinder, cutting a small square
A rotary hammer on its hammer setting
A wood spade bit in an impact driver
A step drill in a cordless drill

questions.stem: Holes are to be drilled in an enclosure that already has breakers fitted inside. What should be done to protect them?
options: Cover the devices and catch or vacuum the swarf
Switch the panel on so swarf is blown out
Drill faster so less swarf is made
Leave the swarf, as it cannot conduct

questions.stem: Before you let a trainee use the team's core drill on site, what must you be sure of?
options: They were trained and you watched them use it
They have used a hand drill at home before
They have read the price list for core bits
They are the strongest member of the team

questions.stem: A rotary hammer kicks back and sprains a worker's wrist. After first aid, what should the team leader do?
options: Carry on with the job using the same tool and method
Throw the tool away and say nothing about it
Blame the worker so the job is not held up
Report it, check the tool and review the method

questions.stem: Several tools are used from one extension lead with a multi-outlet box. What is the main risk?
options: The tools will each run at a lower speed
The lead and box may be overloaded and overheat
The RCD will stop all of the tools from starting
The tools will drain each other's batteries

questions.stem: Which tool is best for cutting a neat rectangular opening in plasterboard for a flush box?
options: An angle grinder with a stone disc
A rotary hammer with a chisel bit
A plasterboard saw or an oscillating tool
A wet diamond core drill with a large bit

questions.stem: Why are cordless tools often preferred for second-fix work in finished buildings?
options: They always have more power than corded tools
Their batteries never need to be charged
No trailing leads to trip over or damage
They do not need any checks before use

questions.stem: Which PPE is needed when cutting steel strut with an angle grinder?
options: Eye and face protection, hearing protection and gloves
A dust mask only, since grinding sparks cannot harm you
Sunglasses and a cap with a peak
Rubber gloves only, to protect from shock

questions.stem: Why should every tool issued to the team be signed out and back in on a tool register?
options: So the tools can be charged to the client
So the tools are used only once each
So the store does not need a lock
So missing or damaged tools are traced

questions.stem: A corded tool's RCD trips each time the tool is started on a wet morning. What should you do?
options: Bypass the RCD so the work can carry on
Stop using it and have the tool and lead checked
Keep resetting it until the tool keeps on running
Swap it to a bigger breaker that will not trip

questions.stem: How should concrete dust be cleaned up after drilling and chasing?
options: Dry sweep it with a stiff broom
Blow it away with compressed air
Vacuum it with a suitable dust extractor
Leave it for the building's cleaners next day

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name of the chuck system used on rotary hammers, where the bit slides in and is held by grooves in its shank?
What type of bit, a hollow tube with diamond segments on its end, cuts large round holes in concrete?
What is the name of the power tool with two diamond blades side by side that cuts slots in walls for conduit?
Which mineral dust from concrete and block can cause the lung disease silicosis?
A 110 V tool is rated 1 320 W. What current does it draw, in amps?
What is the name of the adjustable ring on a drill-driver that slips at a set tightness so that screws are not over-driven?
Which electrical test checks the earth path from the metal casing of an earthed (Class I) tool to the earth pin of its plug?
What is the name of the cord that ties a tool to the worker or the platform so that it cannot fall?
What machine cuts threads on the ends of steel conduit, using dies held in a head?
What do the letters Li-ion stand for on a tool battery?
What is the name for the sudden, violent twist or jump of a power tool when its bit or blade binds?
What is the name of the base that holds a core drill rigid against the wall or floor while it cuts?
A drill runs at 600 rev/min. How many revolutions does it make in 15 seconds?
What name is given to the small metal chips and curls made when drilling or cutting metal?
What is the name of the hand-held power tool whose blade moves rapidly from side to side, used to cut openings in plasterboard and trim in tight spots?

essays.stem: Your team will run conduit through block walls and fix it to concrete ceilings in a school while classes continue nearby. Describe how you would plan the use of power tools for this job.
essays.modelAnswer: I would visit the site, study the drawings and talk to the principal to agree working times and areas, so noisy and dusty work is done when classes are not next door. I would write a risk assessment and method statement covering the tools, the hazards and the controls. I would choose suitable tools: a rotary hammer with SDS bits and core bits for the wall holes, with dust extraction, and cordless drills for fixings. I would check for hidden services with a detector and drawings. For the ceiling work I would plan safe access, such as a mobile platform with guard rails, and tool lanyards. All corded tools would be in date for inspection and testing, and fed through RCD or GFCI protection. I would fence off the work area with signs to keep students out, and plan PPE: eye and hearing protection and dust masks. Finally I would brief the team and check they are trained on each tool.
markingPoints: Agrees times and areas with the school; reads drawings
Written risk assessment and method statement
Right tools chosen with dust extraction; hidden services checked
Safe access for ceiling work, tool lanyards, RCD-protected and tested tools
Barriers and signs, PPE, team briefing and training

essays.stem: Describe the checks a user should make on a corded power tool and its extension lead before use, and explain how this differs from the formal inspection and test done at set intervals.
essays.modelAnswer: Before each use, the user looks at the whole tool and lead with the plug out. They check that the plug is not cracked or burnt and its pins are straight, that the cable is not cut, crushed or taped, and that the outer sheath is held firmly where it enters the plug and the tool. They check the casing is not cracked, the guards and side handles are fitted, the switch works and springs back, and the tool has a label showing it is in date for testing. The extension lead is checked in the same way, and its rating must suit the tool. The RCD's test button is pressed to check it trips. The formal inspection and test is done at set intervals by a competent person. It includes a more detailed inspection, opening the plug, and electrical tests such as earth continuity and insulation resistance with a suitable tester. The results are recorded and the tool is labelled.
markingPoints: Plug, pins and cable checked with the tool unplugged
Casing, guards, handle and switch checked
Test label in date; lead rating suits the tool; RCD test button
Formal inspection is by a competent person at set intervals
Formal test includes electrical tests and records with a label

essays.stem: Describe how to set up and use a diamond core drill to cut a 110 mm hole through a concrete wall for a cable duct.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check the drawings and scan the wall for cables, pipes and steel, and get approval to drill. I check the core drill, bit and leads, and make sure the supply has RCD or GFCI protection as the maker says, especially if water is used. I mark the hole centre on both sides. I fix the drill stand to the wall with the anchor or vacuum base the maker recommends, so the drill cannot twist, and set the bit square to the wall. I arrange to catch the water and slurry, and protect the area and anything below. On the far side I fence off the area, as the core can drop out. I wear eye and hearing protection, gloves and boots. I start the drill slowly to begin the cut, then feed steadily without forcing it. If the bit binds, I stop and free it. When through, I remove the core safely, clean up and deburr the hole.
markingPoints: Checks drawings and scans for services; permission
Checks tool and supply protection (RCD or GFCI) as the maker says
Fixes the stand securely, bit square to the wall
Controls water and slurry; fences off the far side; PPE
Starts slowly, steady feed, frees a binding bit, cleans up

essays.stem: Explain the health risk from dust when drilling and chasing concrete and block, and describe how you would control it on a job.
essays.modelAnswer: Concrete and block contain crystalline silica. Drilling, chasing and cutting make very fine dust that can be breathed deep into the lungs. Over time it can cause silicosis, a disease that scars the lungs and cannot be cured, and it is linked to other lung diseases. The dust is often too fine to see. The best control is to make less dust: plan routes so fewer chases are needed, or use surface conduit or trunking. Where cutting is needed, tools should have on-tool extraction connected to a suitable vacuum, or use water to keep the dust down where the tool is made for it. The area should be ventilated and closed off from other people. Workers wear a close-fitting dust respirator of the right rating, and are trained to fit it. Dust is cleaned up with a vacuum, never by dry sweeping or blowing. Time spent on dusty work can also be shared out.
markingPoints: Names silica and silicosis (lasting lung damage)
Explains fine dust is breathed in and often not seen
Reduce dust at source: plan routes, extraction or water
Ventilate, close off the area, wear a suitable fitted respirator
Clean up by vacuum, not sweeping or blowing; limit exposure time

essays.stem: Choose the best power tool for each of these tasks and say why: cutting steel strut channel; making a 25 mm hole in a fitted steel enclosure; drilling 8 mm fixing holes in a concrete ceiling; cutting an opening in plasterboard for a box; tightening breaker terminals.
essays.modelAnswer: For steel strut, a portable band saw with a metal blade is best: it cuts square and clean, with few sparks and little noise, so no hot-work permit is usually needed. For a 25 mm hole in a fitted enclosure, a step drill in a cordless drill, or a knockout punch after a pilot hole, gives a clean round hole; the parts inside are covered so swarf does not get in. For 8 mm holes in a concrete ceiling, a rotary hammer with an SDS bit and depth stop is used from a stable platform, with dust extraction and eye protection. For a plasterboard opening, an oscillating tool or a plasterboard saw cuts a neat rectangle without cracking the board. For breaker terminals, a torque screwdriver set to the maker's figure is used, not an impact driver, because the terminals need the right torque: too loose overheats, too tight cracks the terminal.
markingPoints: Band saw for strut, with reason
Step drill or punch for the enclosure hole, protecting the inside
Rotary hammer with SDS bit and depth stop for the ceiling
Oscillating tool or plasterboard saw for the opening
Torque screwdriver for terminals, with the reason

essays.stem: Describe how you would use a battery hydraulic crimping tool to fit a lug to a large copper cable, and how you would check the finished crimp.
essays.modelAnswer: First I make sure the cable is isolated and proved dead if it is connected to anything, or that I am working on a new cable end. I check the lug matches the conductor size and material and the stud size, and choose the die marked for that lug size, as the tool maker's chart shows. I check the tool and battery are in good order. I strip the insulation to the length of the lug barrel, without nicking the strands, and push the conductor fully into the barrel. I fit the die, place the lug in the jaws at the position the maker shows, keep my fingers clear and trigger the tool until it completes its full cycle and releases. Some lugs need more than one crimp along the barrel. To check, I look for a full, even crimp with the die marks visible, no strands outside, the conductor showing at the inspection hole, and no cracks. I give it a firm pull test and record it if required.
markingPoints: Cable dead or new; lug matches size and material
Correct die from the maker's chart; tool checked
Strips to the right length without damage; conductor fully in
Crimps at the right place with fingers clear, full cycle
Checks crimp: marks, no strands out, no cracks, pull test

essays.stem: Explain how to cut a thread safely on a length of steel conduit with a power threading machine.
essays.modelAnswer: I read the maker's instructions and check the machine: guards, foot switch, cable and plug, and that the supply is protected by an RCD or GFCI. I set the machine on firm, level ground and support long lengths of conduit on a stand so they do not whip or tip. I cut the conduit square and ream the inside to remove the burr. I fit the correct die head for the conduit size and set it to the right thread length. I make sure the oil reservoir is full so cutting oil flows over the dies. I clamp the conduit in the chuck, stand at the foot switch, and run the machine, closing the die head onto the conduit. When the thread is cut, I open the die head, stop the machine with the foot switch and remove the conduit. I wear safety glasses and gloves when handling the conduit, but keep loose gloves and clothing away from the turning chuck. Finally I wipe off the oil, check the thread with a coupler, and clean up the swarf.
markingPoints: Checks machine, guards, foot switch and protected supply
Supports long lengths; cuts square and reams
Right die head and thread length; cutting oil
Uses foot switch; keeps loose items away from the chuck
Checks the thread and cleans up oil and swarf

essays.stem: Your team will spend two weeks chasing and drilling block walls. Explain how you would plan the work to limit the team's exposure to noise and vibration.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would look for ways to do less of the noisy, vibrating work: for example, using surface trunking where it is allowed, or planning routes to need fewer chases and holes. I would choose tools with lower vibration and noise ratings, and keep them in good condition with sharp bits and blades, because blunt bits vibrate more and take longer. I would use the maker's vibration and noise figures to estimate how long each person can safely use each tool in a day. I would share the work out so no one person uses the chaser or rotary hammer all day, swapping with quieter tasks. Everyone would wear hearing protection in the noisy area, and signs would mark it. I would remind the team to let the tool do the work without gripping too hard, to take breaks, and to keep warm and dry. Anyone with tingling, numbness or white fingers should report it at once.
markingPoints: Reduce the work: fewer chases or other methods
Choose low-vibration tools; keep bits sharp and tools maintained
Limit time on each tool using maker's data; rotate tasks
Hearing protection and signed noisy areas
Train on grip and breaks; report early symptoms

essays.stem: As team leader, explain how you would make sure the trainees in your team use power tools safely and well on a site job.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the job, I find out what each trainee has been trained on and is allowed to use. Nobody uses a tool they have not been trained on, especially core drills, threading machines and cartridge tools. For a new tool, I explain and show how to use it, its guards and its PPE, then watch the trainee use it on a practice piece before real work. I brief the whole team on the method statement, the risk assessment and the site rules at the start of each day. I check tools are inspected and in date and that RCD protection is in place. During the work I watch how they use the tools and correct unsafe habits at once, such as a missing side handle or a guard taken off, explaining why. I praise good work too. At the end of the day, tools are checked, cleaned and signed back in. Any incident or near miss is reported and talked through so the team learns from it.
markingPoints: Checks each trainee's training; only trained people use each tool
Demonstrates, then watches the trainee use the tool
Daily briefing on method statement and rules; tools checked and protected
Supervises, corrects unsafe habits with reasons, gives feedback
End-of-day checks; incidents and near misses reported and discussed

essays.stem: While drilling a wall with a corded rotary hammer, a trainee hits a hidden cable. There is a bang and the breaker trips, but nobody is hurt. Explain what you would do straight away and afterwards.
essays.modelAnswer: Straight away I would tell the trainee to let go of the drill and step back, and keep everyone away. I would treat the cable and the drill as live until proven otherwise. I would find and isolate the circuit, lock it off and tag it, and prove it dead with a tester checked before and after. I would check the trainee for burns or shock and arrange medical checks, as shock can have delayed effects. Then I would make the area safe, take the drill out of use for inspection and test, and report the incident to my supervisor. Afterwards, the damaged cable would be repaired properly, tested and recorded before the circuit is switched on again. I would investigate why it happened: were the drawings checked, was a detector used, was the cable in a safe zone? I would update the method statement and brief the team on what to do differently, such as scanning every hole position.
markingPoints: Gets everyone clear; treats cable and drill as live
Isolates, locks off and proves dead
Checks the trainee and arranges medical checks
Reports; takes drill out of use; repairs and tests the cable
Investigates the cause and updates the method; briefs the team

practical1.title: Plan and make conduit penetrations and fixings in a block practice wall
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group a short job on a block practice wall at the Centre: drill three 25–32 mm holes through the wall for conduit, cut one short chase (or line of holes) with dust extraction, and fix a 1 m length of strut channel to the wall with suitable anchors. As a group, first write a short risk assessment and method statement, and choose the tools. Each member checks one tool and its lead before use and records it on the check sheet; the assessor presses the RCD test button with the group. Scan the wall and mark the positions. Then each member drills at least one hole or fixing with the rotary hammer while another member runs the extractor and a third watches the area. Finish by cleaning up with the vacuum, checking the work against the marked positions, and recording the tools as returned and checked.
materials: Block practice wall at the Centre
Rotary hammer with SDS bits (and a core bit if available), with on-tool dust extraction and a suitable vacuum
Cordless drill-driver, strut channel, anchors and fixings
Cable and pipe detector, tape, level and marker
RCD-protected supply, inspected leads and tool check sheet
PPE: safety glasses, hearing protection, close-fitting dust respirators, gloves, boots
photos: The written risk assessment and method statement
The wall being scanned and the positions marked
A member drilling with the extractor working
The area after cleaning with the vacuum
checklist: Helped write the risk assessment and method statement
Checked a tool and lead correctly and recorded it
Wore the right PPE, including a fitted dust respirator
Used the rotary hammer correctly: right mode, side handle, depth stop, steady feed
Used dust extraction and kept others out of the work area
Fixed or helped fix the strut level and secure
Cleaned up with the vacuum, not by sweeping or blowing
safety: All corded tools are in date for testing and fed through an RCD or GFCI tested at the start
Scan for hidden services before drilling; the practice wall has no live cables
Wear eye and hearing protection and a fitted dust respirator while drilling and chasing
Keep the side handle on and the depth stop set; unplug before changing bits

practical2.title: Build a strut frame and fit out an enclosure with power tools
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the group a drawing of a small strut-channel frame that holds a steel enclosure, and two short lengths of large cable (not connected to anything) that need lugs. As a group, plan the work and share the tasks. Members take turns to cut strut lengths with a portable band saw and deburr them, drill and fit the enclosure's holes with a step drill or a knockout punch after a pilot hole, and assemble the frame with a cordless driver. Two members crimp lugs onto the cable ends with a hydraulic crimping tool, using the right die, and the group checks each crimp. Fix the cable tails to a terminal block in the enclosure and tighten them with a torque screwdriver set to the maker's figure. Every member uses at least two different power tools. Finish with an inspection of the frame and enclosure against the drawing, and a post-use check of every tool.
materials: Strut channel, brackets and fixings, and a drawing of the frame
Small steel enclosure with a terminal block inside
Two short lengths of large copper cable and matching lugs (not connected to any supply)
Portable band saw, cordless drill-driver, step drill or knockout punch set, hydraulic crimping tool with dies, torque screwdriver
Files and deburring tools, vacuum for swarf
Tool check sheets and an inspection sheet
photos: The tool check sheets completed before use
Strut being cut with the band saw, with the work clamped
A hole being made in the enclosure, with the inside covered
The hydraulic crimping tool with the right die and lug
A finished crimp next to the die chart
The torque screwdriver set to the maker's figure
checklist: Checked their tools before use and recorded it
Clamped or supported the work properly before cutting or drilling
Used at least two power tools correctly and safely
Chose the right die and made a sound crimp, or checked one
Tightened terminals to the maker's torque with a torque screwdriver
Kept swarf out of the enclosure and cleaned up
Checked the finished work against the drawing
